title: Writing for Armstrong after 1935: Cavalier Rusty Cannon and the Old Man Mose record
summary: He wrote Armstrong an arrangement but regretted writing the piano solo; the Armstrong-Russell Old Man Mose record played just one note.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: Did you ever write anything more for Louis, or what was your relationship with Louis after he went to New York and took Louis Russell band?
Well, no, I never did. Yes, I wrote -- Louis wanted me to write for him, and which I made the arrangement, on -- he wanted me to make an arrangement on Cavalier Rusty Cannon.

And I made it for him. But I made a mistake by writing out the piano part, by writing the piano solo. Because Louis Russell told me I should haven't written the piano solo. I don't know why. Well, I just wanted the solo to go that way.
Because I heard the band to doing, and I just wanted it to go that way. And -- I don't know what
The record that Louis made of Old Man Mose, was that your arrangement or did Louis Russell arrange that?
Now, that I don't know. Louis didn't play my arrangement, because as I said, they really didn't play the 'Old Man Mose.'
No, they played just the straight, same note, just -- should have been named Old Man Mose One Note. You know, like Johnny One Note?
Well, that should have been 'Old Man Mose One Note', because they just took that same note and carried it all the way through.
